record.ear: Fair and colder. High 30. Low 19. Ice re-forming in the coves.

lead.headline: Queens Light & Power publishes a notice that its works make no tone
lead.deck: Paid notice of 212 words in five borough papers; the company 'aware of no hum'; Alderman Feeney replies by letter at 4:10 p.m.
lead.body: Queens Light & Power yesterday published a paid notice of 212 words in five borough papers, this one among them, stating that 'the company's plant at Astoria and its lines throughout Queens produce no tone, at 41 cycles or at any other figure.' The notice is signed by Mr. Roland Tisch, chief engineer, and states that the company is 'aware of no hum.' Alderman Feeney replied by letter at 4:10 p.m., enclosing Dr. Rastin's 23 readings. The company did not acknowledge the letter.

columns.headline: Board's refusal on the Riverhead record to go before Justice Rourke
columns.body: Mr. Francis Gorman, for Mr. Walter Pruitt, will ask Justice Thaddeus Rourke to order the Board of Elections to play to counsel the 11 seconds of its Riverhead record, kept sealed by a vote of three to one. The bench warrant for Mr. Joseph Marchetti stands.

columns.headline: Exchange spares at 17 days; second salvage truck due Monday
columns.body: The Queens exchange held 17 days' spare valves last night, the supervisor reports. The second motor truck of the Newark works' salvaged stores is due on Monday. The average call ran 3 minutes 6 seconds. Used valves were 60 cents on Jackson Avenue; eggs 52 cents.

columns.headline: Dr. Strand compares the WORS 1610 carol with 600 Welsh hymn tunes
columns.body: Dr. Matthias Strand of Union Seminary wrote yesterday to the Phonautograph Society that he has compared the carol heard on WORS 1610 with 600 Welsh hymn tunes lent by a Brooklyn chapel, without a match. He has asked the chapel's precentor to hear the record.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The terrier Duke howled at 9:50 p.m. on 31st Street for 11 seconds, Mr. Anton Vrabel reports.

speaker.ear: Fair and colder. High 30. The company says it is quiet out. Listen for yourself.

lead.headline: Light & Power pays to change its tune, and says there isn't one
lead.deck: Two hundred and twelve words at advertising rates to say the works make no tone; Duke of 31st Street howls a reply at ten to ten
lead.body: Queens Light & Power has paid good money, at our rates, which are not low, to tell the borough in print that it makes no tone. Not at forty-one cycles. Not at any figure at all. Mr. Tisch has signed it. We accepted the money and printed every word, in a box with a border, and the box hummed. Alderman Feeney wrote back the same afternoon with Dr. Rastin's twenty-three readings. At ten to ten last night, Duke of 31st Street gave his opinion for eleven seconds.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Does the light company hum?'
columns.body: Sir, the operator works for the telephone company, not the light company, and may say what she likes. She says the light company has bought a notice to say it does not hum. She has never known anybody buy a notice to say they do not snore.

columns.headline: Gorman goes to the judge for the eleven seconds the Board won't play
columns.body: Mr. Gorman will ask Justice Rourke to make the Board of Elections play its sealed eleven seconds. The Board says the count is certified. Mr. Gorman says the count is not the question. Marchetti, who might answer it, remains at large and unrecorded.

columns.headline: Strand runs the carol past six hundred Welsh tunes, and none will pick up
columns.body: Dr. Strand of Union Seminary has played the WORS carol against six hundred Welsh hymn tunes lent by a Brooklyn chapel. None matched. He has asked the chapel's precentor to come and hear it. The precentor says he will bring his own tuning fork, and his own doubts.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Duke howled eleven seconds at ten to ten. The company says it was the wind. The wind has not paid for a notice.

record.ear: Fair and cold. High 28. Low 18. Thaw ended; cutting to resume Monday if the cold holds.

lead.headline: Week's count: ice houses hold 61,400 tons against a summer's 90,000
lead.deck: Five days of thaw stop the harvest 28,600 tons short; the Bowery Bay company asks for 'ten cold days'; summer ice may rise a quarter cent
lead.body: The three Sound ice companies held 61,400 tons in their houses at last night's count, against the 90,000 tons Queens used last summer, the Bowery Bay company reports. Five days of thaw since the 28th have rotted the ice at Whitestone and Willets Point to six inches. Mr. Owen Pratt says the companies need ten cold days to cut the difference and will cut from Monday if the ice reaches nine inches. Without them, he says, the summer price may rise a quarter cent the pound.

columns.headline: Exchange cat's fourth parcel tied with lineman's lacing cord
columns.body: A fourth parcel for 'Party Line, Queens Exchange, Position 43' was delivered yesterday, postmarked Corona, January 31, with a tin of sardines. It was wrapped in plain paper and tied with waxed lacing cord of the kind used by linemen. Detective Sergeant Edward Moran has the cord.

columns.headline: Steinway church sixth on the Newark valve list
columns.body: The First Reformed Church of Steinway is sixth on the Newark works' list for a fifty-watt output valve, the Rev. Martin Ostrander says, three churches ahead of it having been supplied. Members will read tomorrow's sermon by telephone to the shut-ins for a third Sunday.

columns.headline: Listening Act third reading not yet placed on the Assembly calendar
columns.body: Assemblyman Thomas Burkhardt's print of the Listening Act, ordered to third reading on January 22, has not been placed on the calendar. Speaker McGinnies's office says the chamber's record of the gallery 'is still being listened to.' The voice heard at 2:51 p.m. is not identified.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Queens exchange reports the average call this week at 3 minutes 4 seconds.

speaker.ear: Cold again. High 28. Groundhog Day. The groundhog has not called in.

lead.headline: Groundhog won't come to the phone, and the ice men are left on hold
lead.deck: Punxsutawney's weather prophet is not on the exchange; Mr. Pratt needs ten cold days and is praying to anything with fur
lead.body: Today, in a town in Pennsylvania, a groundhog comes out of a hole and tells the nation whether to expect six more weeks of winter. We tried to put a call through. Punxsutawney has an exchange, but the groundhog is not on it. This is a pity, because Mr. Pratt of Bowery Bay needs ten cold days, and has twenty-eight thousand six hundred tons of summer still out on the Sound turning to slush. If the groundhog sees his shadow, the ice men will stand him a drink.

columns.headline: Party Line's fourth tin comes tied up in a lineman's knot
columns.body: Tin number four reached the exchange cat yesterday, Corona postmark, sardines inside, tied with waxed lacing cord, the kind the telephone men use to dress their cables. Sergeant Moran kept the string. He left the sardines. Party Line has formed her own opinion of the Sergeant.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Sixty-three pins and counting on the Speaker's wall
columns.body: The WORS map on our office wall now carries sixty-three pins, one for every reader who heard the station and wrote. Monday we print it. Our engraver says it is the hardest map he has ever cut, being a map of a thing that is not there.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: a Bayside musicale goes ahead with the set switched off
columns.body: Darlings, a Bayside hostess with no valves to spare gave her Thursday musicale the old way, with a piano and a nephew. The nephew played for an hour. Several guests asked whether he could be switched off. He could not. He is twelve.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Three minutes four, the week's average call. Queens can say goodbye in under a minute now. Mothers excepted.

editorial.headline: Fifty dollars for her name; three hundred ladies claim it
editorial.body: Last Saturday this paper offered fifty dollars to any reader who could bring us the true name of the woman who calls herself Lilith. By Thursday three hundred and twelve women had called at our offices on Borden Avenue, each declaring herself to be Lilith and asking for the fifty dollars, which she proposed to spend on her children's shoes, her sister's rent, the Women's Trade Union League or, in one case, a new hat. They queued around the block. They sang. Our switchboard girl joined them at lunch. We have withdrawn the offer. We say this: a joke is not a confession, and three hundred women laughing at an editor is not evidence of anything but bad upbringing.

record.ear: Cloudy and cold. High 27. Low 19. Snow flurries.

lead.headline: Brooklyn precentor hears the WORS 1610 carol and cannot place it
lead.deck: Mr. Evan Pritchard of the Welsh Congregational chapel listens three times at Union Seminary; says he has 'sung it, but not in this country'; Dr. Strand to write to Aberystwyth
lead.body: Mr. Evan Pritchard, precentor of the Welsh Congregational chapel in Brooklyn, heard the record of the carol received on WORS 1610 on Christmas night three times yesterday at Union Seminary, at Dr. Matthias Strand's invitation. He told Dr. Strand that he had 'sung it, but not in this country,' and could give neither its name nor where. He is 71 and came from Merthyr in 1882. Dr. Strand will write to the National Library at Aberystwyth. The record remains with the Seminary until Easter.

columns.headline: Steinway church reads its sermon by telephone a third Sunday
columns.body: Members of the First Reformed Church of Steinway will read the Rev. Martin Ostrander's sermon by telephone today to the church's 212 shut-ins for a third Sunday. The exchange has asked readers to begin at noon in the alphabetical order of the shut-ins' names.

columns.headline: Coal holds at 15 dollars; deliveries resume on the Long Island City hills
columns.body: The Long Island City coal yards report deliveries resumed on the hills after the thaw, with 52 horses out yesterday. Coal holds at 15 dollars the ton. The Vernon Avenue yard reports the Percheron Dutchman 'well and opinionated.'

columns.headline: Little America reports 9 below and the Fairchild housed for the winter
columns.body: Commander Byrd's operator reported last night 9 below zero at Little America and the Fairchild monoplane housed in a snow hangar. The message was played at 10 in the Record's window to 260. The ships are to sail north about February 20.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Pritchard asked that the carol record not be played a fourth time while he was in the room.

speaker.ear: Grey, flurries. High 27. Sunday. The telephones are going to church again.

lead.headline: Brooklyn's Welsh precentor knows the carol, but he can't place the call
lead.deck: Seventy-one years old and fifty of them singing; he says he has sung it, but not here, and would rather not hear it a fourth time
lead.body: Mr. Evan Pritchard has been precentor of the Welsh chapel in Brooklyn since before the elevated, and there is not a hymn in Wales he cannot lead from memory. Dr. Strand sat him down yesterday and played him the WORS carol. He listened three times with his hat on his knee. Then he said he had sung it, but not in this country, and asked them please not to play it again while he was in the room. They did not. Dr. Strand is writing to Wales.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Why ring the shut-ins alphabetically?'
columns.body: Madam, because two hundred members ringing two hundred shut-ins at noon is a traffic jam, and the alphabet is the only queue everybody agrees on. If your name is Zimmerman, you will hear the sermon at a quarter to three. It is the same sermon. It keeps.

columns.headline: Dutchman back in harness, and the hills of Long Island City get an earful
columns.body: The Percheron Dutchman is hauling coal again on the Long Island City hills, the thaw being over. The yard reports him well and opinionated. He has views on the Vernon Avenue grade, which he expresses at the bottom of it, loudly, before going up.

columns.headline: Byrd puts his plane to bed, and the Barrier signs off at nine below
columns.body: The Commander has tucked his Fairchild into a hangar of snow at Little America, at nine below. It will sleep until spring, which down there is October. Two hundred and sixty stood in the cold at the Record's window to hear this. We admire them. We stayed in.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Pritchard went home by the elevated and was not heard to sing.

record.ear: Fair and colder. High 25. Low 14. Ice nine inches at Whitestone by Tuesday.

lead.headline: Athletic Club five lose to the Brooklyn Visitations 36 to 24 before 2,400
lead.deck: Largest crowd at the armory this season, 300 turned away; Mr. Dillon held to four; game broadcast to St. John's Hospital at the patients' request
lead.body: The Brooklyn Visitations beat the Long Island City Athletic Club five 36 to 24 at the armory on Saturday night before 2,400, the largest crowd of the season, 300 being turned away at the door. Mr. Frank Dillon was held to four points. The game was broadcast by the armory's transmitter at the request of the patients of St. John's Hospital in Long Island City, who had written to ask. The club stands at eight wins and six losses and plays the Newark Turners on Saturday.

columns.headline: Kissena Lake reopens to skaters; Flushing seven beat Bayside 3 to 2
columns.body: Kissena Lake reopened to skaters on Saturday at nine inches, and the Flushing seven beat Bayside 3 to 2 there yesterday before 400. The referee used a hand-bell throughout, by agreement of both captains. Skating continues while the ice holds.

columns.headline: Second Newark salvage truck to leave at 6 this morning
columns.body: The second motor truck of the Newark works' salvaged valves is to leave at 6 this morning with 580 sleeves, 380 of them for the Queens exchange, the supervisor reports. The three-minute request continues. The trade will receive 'the remainder, if any.'

columns.headline: Mr. Gorman files his petition on the Riverhead record's 11 seconds
columns.body: Mr. Francis Gorman filed with Justice Thaddeus Rourke on Saturday a petition that the Board of Elections be directed to play to counsel the 11 seconds of its Riverhead record sealed on January 30. Argument is set for Thursday at 10. Chairman Delaney will oppose.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Bowery Bay company will cut at Whitestone from 7 a.m. Tuesday if the ice holds at nine inches.

speaker.ear: Fair and colder. High 25. The ice men are smiling. Avert your eyes.

lead.headline: Where's WORS? The Speaker pins down a station that won't stay put
lead.deck: Sixty-three sightings from November to Saturday, on page four, a pin for each; the transmitter is not on it, and neither, the Radio Division says, is anything else
lead.body: Here it is, readers: the Speaker's map of WORS 1610, on page four, sixty-three pins, one for every one of you who heard it and wrote in. Hell Gate has nine. Maspeth has six. Woodside has a milkman and his horse. Kew Gardens has a burnt piece of toast. Mr. Pike of the Radio Division saw the proof on Saturday and said the pins are 'very nicely placed' and 'tell us nothing.' He kept a copy. Send us yours. The station is out there. So are we.

columns.headline: Visitations ring up thirty-six, and the Club five are out of range
columns.body: The Brooklyn Visitations beat the Athletic Club five 36 to 24 before twenty-four hundred, with three hundred more outside listening at the doors. Dillon got four. The game went out over the air to the patients at St. John's, who cheered for Brooklyn to annoy the nurses.

columns.headline: Kissena reopens, and the ref rings in the new ice
columns.body: Kissena Lake is open again at nine inches, and the Flushing seven beat Bayside 3 to 2 there yesterday. The referee went straight to the hand-bell this time, by agreement. Hockey in Queens is now played to a sound like a school yard at nine o'clock.

columns.headline: Gorman asks the court to let the Board's eleven seconds speak up
columns.body: Mr. Gorman has asked Justice Rourke to make the Board of Elections play its eleven sealed seconds, and the Justice will hear him on Thursday. Chairman Delaney will oppose. Nobody in Queens has argued so long about eleven seconds since the last time a lady was asked her age.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Pike of the Radio Division has asked for three more copies of the map. For the office, he says.

record.ear: Fair and cold. High 24. Low 13. Cutting at Whitestone from 7 a.m.

lead.headline: Assembly puts over the third reading of the Listening Act to March 5
lead.deck: Speaker McGinnies's motion carried 81 to 62; the gallery record of January 22 under examination by the Clerk; the voice at 2:51 p.m. compared with some forty visitors
lead.body: The Assembly yesterday voted 81 to 62 to put over the third reading of Assemblyman Thomas Burkhardt's print of the Listening Act to March 5, on the motion of Speaker Joseph McGinnies. The Speaker told the chamber that the Clerk is still examining the record of the gallery of January 22, and has compared the voice heard at 2:51 p.m. with those of some forty visitors who consented to be recorded, without a match. Assemblyman Kilbride asked whether any visitor had resented being recorded. The record notes laughter.

columns.headline: Dance marathon to open tonight at the Jamaica Arena to a recorded band
columns.body: A dance marathon for a prize of 1,000 dollars opens at 8 tonight at the Jamaica Arena with 64 couples entered. Music will be supplied by records of the Harmony Kings orchestra 'without interval, for the duration.' A Health Department nurse will attend.

columns.headline: Ice cutting resumes on the Sound at nine inches; 300 men out
columns.body: The Bowery Bay and Whitestone ice companies resume cutting at 7 this morning with 300 men, the Whitestone field having reached nine inches yesterday. Mr. Owen Pratt says the companies need 28,600 tons and 'about ten days of this.'

columns.headline: Second salvage truck brings 380 sleeves; exchange spares at 21 days
columns.body: The second Newark salvage truck reached the Queens exchange at 10:50 a.m. yesterday with 380 sleeves of valves, bringing its spares to 21 days. The three-minute request continues 'until the works are making again,' the supervisor says. Used valves were 55 cents.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Ambrose Tully, for the real estate owners, wired Speaker McGinnies 'congratulations on March.'

speaker.ear: Fair and cold. High 24. The ice men are back on the Sound and back in good humour.

lead.headline: Albany puts the Listening Act on hold till March and replays the gallery
lead.deck: Forty visitors have read into a machine for the Clerk; none of them is the voice that said 'resent'; Kilbride asks if anyone resented the asking
lead.body: The Assembly has put the Listening Act over to March, eighty-one to sixty-two, because the Clerk has not finished listening to the gallery. Forty visitors from January 22 have said the word 'resent' into the Clerk's machine. None of them is the voice. Mr. Kilbride rose to ask if any of them had resented it, and the chamber laughed, and the chamber's record laughed with it. Somewhere in the State a person with a very particular way of saying one word is keeping quiet.

columns.headline: Sixty-four couples to dance till they drop, and the band never will
columns.body: The Jamaica Arena dance marathon opens tonight at eight, a thousand dollars to the last couple standing, and the band is the Harmony Kings on copper, which neither sleeps nor sweats nor asks for a raise. The couples will do all three by Thursday.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Can I enter the marathon by telephone?'
columns.body: Sir, no. The rules require two feet per entrant on the Arena floor, and an operator cannot connect feet. You may, however, ring the Arena to ask after your sweetheart. Keep it to three minutes. She will be busy.

columns.headline: Ice men cut again, and Mr. Pratt is chilled to the bone with joy
columns.body: Three hundred men went out on the Whitestone field this morning at nine inches, and Mr. Pratt was with them in two coats. He wants ten days of this. Queens wants ten days of anything else. The Sound has the casting vote.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Tully of the landlords wired the Speaker of the Assembly 'congratulations on March.' March is not taking calls.

record.ear: Fair and cold. High 26. Low 15. Northwest wind.

lead.headline: Dance marathon opens at Jamaica with 64 couples and a band on record
lead.deck: Floor opened at 8:02 p.m.; 1,900 spectators at 25 cents; first couple out at 1:40 a.m.; the Harmony Kings' records in a rotation of six hours
lead.body: The dance marathon at the Jamaica Arena opened at 8:02 p.m. yesterday with 64 couples on the floor and 1,900 spectators in the stands at 25 cents. Music is supplied by records of the Harmony Kings orchestra, played in a rotation of six hours through the Arena's system. The management states that the band 'will not tire.' The first couple, from Richmond Hill, left the floor at 1:40 a.m. A Health Department nurse is on duty, and couples rest 15 minutes in the hour.

columns.headline: Sergeant Moran asks an evening paper the source of an engraving
columns.body: Detective Sergeant Edward Moran called yesterday at the Loud Speaker, an evening paper, to ask the source of its engraving of January 12 showing a tall woman in a fur coat at Corona. The engraver stated it was drawn 'from a reader's description, given by telephone.'

columns.headline: Queens Light & Power declines Alderman Feeney's request to meet
columns.body: Queens Light & Power declined by letter yesterday Alderman Feeney's request for a meeting on the Hum, stating that the company 'has published its position and has nothing to add.' The letter was three lines. The Alderman has sent it to Commissioner Lacey.

columns.headline: Sorrentino and Lusk matched again for February 23 at Ridgewood Grove
columns.body: Kid Sorrentino of Astoria will meet Harry Lusk of Jersey City again in ten rounds at Ridgewood Grove on February 23, the promoter announced. Mr. Lusk's manager has dropped his request for the record of the seventh round of their January bout 'in favour of a new seventh.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Sixty couples remained on the Arena floor at 3 a.m., the management reports.

speaker.ear: Fair and cold. High 26. Sixty couples in Jamaica have not yet noticed.

lead.headline: Marathon band is a record that never skips a beat, and Jamaica's feet know it
lead.deck: Sixty-four couples, six hours of Harmony Kings on copper played round and round, and a Richmond Hill pair who lasted till twenty to two
lead.body: At two minutes past eight last night the Harmony Kings struck up at the Jamaica Arena, or rather their record did, and sixty-four couples began to dance for a thousand dollars. The Kings themselves are in Chicago. Their music is in Jamaica, six hours of it, to be played round and round until the last couple drops. By one in the morning the dancers knew every tune. By two they knew every scratch. A Richmond Hill pair went home at twenty to two, waltzing. The record has not noticed.

columns.headline: Sergeant Moran calls on the Speaker, and we draw a blank
columns.body: Sergeant Moran came in yesterday about our engraving of the 12th, the tall woman in the fur coat at Corona. Our engraver told him he drew her from a reader's description over the telephone. The Sergeant asked which reader. So did we. The engraver did not take a name.

columns.headline: Light company says it has nothing to add, and adds three lines
columns.body: Alderman Feeney asked Queens Light & Power for a meeting on the hum. The company wrote back that it has published its position and has nothing to add. That ran to three lines. The Alderman has sent them to the Commission, which now has the company's silence in writing.

columns.headline: Sorrentino and Lusk sign again, and round seven gets a second ring
columns.body: Kid Sorrentino and Harry Lusk meet again at Ridgewood Grove on the 23rd. Lusk's manager has given up asking for the record of the old seventh round and says he wants a new one instead. The promoter has promised to record that too, slowly.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Fifty-five couples at six tonight. The Harmony Kings have played the same foxtrot nine times and it was lovely every time.

record.ear: Cloudy, colder. High 22. Low 10. Snow tonight.

lead.headline: Third lien notice stays up under a Borough watchman; its screws found changed
lead.deck: Mr. Haas posts the notice at 4 p.m. Tuesday with four brass screws; the watchman's record carries four minutes of a screwdriver from 3:10 a.m.; four steel screws in place at 7
lead.body: Mr. Ludwig Haas screwed a third notice of lien to the north door of the Vantry Arcade with four brass screws at 4 p.m. on Tuesday and posted a Borough watchman with a recording set on the pavement until morning. At 7 a.m. yesterday the notice was in place. Its four screws were steel. The watchman's record carries, from 3:10 a.m., four minutes of a screwdriver at work. The watchman states that he was awake and saw no one.

columns.headline: Marathon: 52 couples remain after 28 hours; 14 treated for blisters
columns.body: Fifty-two couples remained on the floor of the Jamaica Arena at midnight, 28 hours after the marathon opened, the management reports. Spectators numbered 2,600 on Wednesday evening. The Health Department nurse treated 14 dancers for blisters. The Harmony Kings' records have been played four times through.

columns.headline: Justice Rourke hears the Riverhead petition at 10 today
columns.body: Justice Thaddeus Rourke will hear at 10 this morning Mr. Francis Gorman's petition that the Board of Elections play to counsel the 11 seconds of its Riverhead record. Chairman Delaney will appear for the Board. Commissioner Wallach has filed an affidavit supporting the petition.

columns.headline: Gettysburg Address to be read at Borough Hall on Lincoln's Birthday
columns.body: The Borough President's office states that the Gettysburg Address will be read at noon on Tuesday from the steps of Borough Hall by the Rev. Martin Ostrander, and recorded. No record of President Lincoln's voice exists, the instrument having been invented in 1873.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The number of Signal Ground Rents Inc. at 120 Broadway was rung again at 11 p.m. at Mr. Haas's request; no reply.

speaker.ear: Colder. Snow tonight. High 22. Somebody in Long Island City owns a screwdriver.

lead.headline: Borough's watchman holds the line all night, and the screws change anyway
lead.deck: Mr. Haas posts his third notice with a watchman and a recording set; at seven the notice is up, the brass is steel, and the record has four minutes of turning
lead.body: This time Mr. Haas left a man on the pavement all night with a recording set and a thermos, and the lien notice was still on the Arcade door at seven yesterday. Victory, said the Borough. Then somebody examined the screws. Mr. Haas put up brass. They are steel now. The watchman's record has four minutes of a screwdriver at ten past three, steady and unhurried, and the watchman says he was awake the whole time and saw nobody. Signal Ground Rents does not answer. It does not need to.

columns.headline: The marathon goes round again, and so does the foxtrot
columns.body: Fifty-two couples were on their feet at the Jamaica Arena at midnight, twenty-eight hours in. The Harmony Kings have been through their six hours four times. The nurse has treated fourteen for blisters. The record has no blisters. It has a groove, which is not the same.

columns.headline: Gorman takes the eleven seconds to Rourke, and Wallach crosses the wires
columns.body: Mr. Gorman argues for the Board's eleven sealed seconds before Justice Rourke this morning. Commissioner Wallach, who lost the Board's vote three to one, has sworn an affidavit on Mr. Gorman's side. A commissioner against his own Board. We have not seen that since the Board was invented.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'What did Lincoln sound like?'
columns.body: Madam, nobody knows. Mr. Lincoln died eight years before the first room was taught to listen, and he did not wait. Mr. Ostrander will read the Gettysburg Address at Borough Hall on Tuesday. It will be recorded. It will sound like Mr. Ostrander.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Snow tonight. The watchman has asked to be posted somewhere warmer, and somewhere nobody else is.

record.ear: Snow, three inches, then clearing and cold. High 20. Low 9.

lead.headline: Newark valve works to resume making Monday; sleeve to fall to 1 dollar 10
lead.deck: One furnace relit Tuesday; first new sleeves to the trade on the 18th; exchange to lift its three-minute request on the 11th
lead.body: The Newark works, closed to manufacture since the fire in January, will resume making receiving valves on Monday from one furnace relit on Tuesday, the company wired last night. The first new sleeves will reach the trade on the 18th at 1 dollar 10, the company states. The Queens exchange will lift its three-minute request on the 11th. The Arcade's hardware counter, which held 9 sleeves at 1 dollar 45 last night, says it has 'taken orders for 300.' Used valves were 50 cents. Eggs are 51 cents.

columns.headline: Justice Rourke reserves decision on the Riverhead record's 11 seconds
columns.body: Justice Thaddeus Rourke reserved decision yesterday on Mr. Francis Gorman's petition after 52 minutes' argument. Chairman Delaney said the Board's record 'is sealed with a certified count and with nothing else.' Mr. Gorman asked: 'Then what is in the eleven seconds?' The Chairman did not answer.

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society meets at 8 tonight on record No. 23
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society of Queens meets at 8 tonight at the Jamaica office, where Mrs. Ottoline Grieve will again move that record No. 23, the Maspeth party's midnight record, be played to members. Mr. Cyril Abbot will speak against the motion.

columns.headline: Marathon: 44 couples after 48 hours; two dancers to hospital
columns.body: Forty-four couples remained on the Jamaica Arena floor at 8 p.m. yesterday, 48 hours after the marathon opened. Two dancers were taken to Mary Immaculate Hospital with exhaustion and discharged. The Health Department has asked that rest periods be lengthened to 20 minutes.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Little America reported 'snow, 14 below, the radio house warm' at 9:50 p.m.

speaker.ear: Snow, then clear and cold. High 20. Newark has struck a light.

lead.headline: Newark lights a furnace, and Queens gets its reception back by the 18th
lead.deck: Valves at a dollar ten on the way, the three-minute rule off from Monday, and the Arcade counter takes orders for three hundred sleeves it hasn't got
lead.body: The Newark works has relit one furnace, and from Monday it will be blowing valves again. New sleeves reach the shops on the 18th at a dollar ten, and the exchange stops asking you to hurry from Monday. Queens may talk again. Queens may say goodbye properly, all four times. The Arcade's counter, with nine sleeves on the shelf at a dollar forty-five, has taken orders for three hundred. The pawnbroker on Jackson Avenue has marked his used valves down to fifty cents and is looking thoughtful.

columns.headline: Rourke reserves on the eleven seconds, and the Board answers in dead air
columns.body: Mr. Gorman asked Chairman Delaney yesterday what is in the Board's eleven sealed seconds, if not the count. The Chairman said nothing at all, which is either an answer or a demonstration. Justice Rourke has reserved. Marchetti has not written.

columns.headline: Mrs. Grieve takes the floor again tonight, and No. 23 waits on the turntable
columns.body: Tonight the Phonautograph Society meets in Jamaica, and Mrs. Grieve will move, for the second time, that the Maspeth midnight record be played. Mr. Abbot will oppose. Last time it was nineteen to eighteen. Bring cocoa. Bring a second cushion.

columns.headline: Forty-four couples, forty-eight hours, and the Harmony Kings never miss a beat
columns.body: Forty-four couples are still dancing at the Jamaica Arena, two have been to Mary Immaculate and back, and the nurse wants twenty minutes' rest in the hour. The band has been through its six hours eight times and is in excellent voice.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Fourteen below at Little America, and the radio house is warm. We knew the radio would get the best room.

record.ear: Fair and cold. High 23. Low 11. Ice twelve inches at Whitestone.

lead.headline: Society divides 19 to 19 on record No. 23; chair's vote keeps it unplayed
lead.deck: Meeting sits 3 hours 5 minutes; Mr. Abbot, presiding, gives the casting vote; the Maspeth party absent; Mrs. Grieve gives notice for March
lead.body: The Phonautograph Society of Queens divided 19 to 19 last night on Mrs. Ottoline Grieve's motion that record No. 23, the Maspeth party's midnight record, be played to members, and Mr. Cyril Abbot, presiding, gave his casting vote against. The meeting sat 3 hours 5 minutes. The three members of the Maspeth party did not attend and sent no letter. Mr. Abbot said the record 'is kept for a year, as I promised, and I keep promises.' Mrs. Grieve gave notice that she will move again in March.

columns.headline: Week's count: 21,700 tons of ice housed in five days of cutting
columns.body: The three Sound ice companies housed 21,700 tons in the five days of cutting to last night, the Bowery Bay company reports, bringing the season to 83,100 tons against the summer's need of 90,000. Mr. Owen Pratt asks for 'three days more.'

columns.headline: Answering doll maker asks for the two returned dolls; toy shop declines
columns.body: The Newark maker of the answering doll wrote on Thursday asking that the two dolls returned by Mrs. Voss and Mrs. Strub be sent to the works. The Vantry Arcade's toy shop has declined, the proprietress stating that the works 'had three already, and said nothing.'

columns.headline: Marathon: 31 couples remain after 72 hours; one disqualified asleep
columns.body: Thirty-one couples remained on the Jamaica Arena floor at 8 p.m. yesterday, 72 hours after the opening. Spectators numbered 3,400. A Woodside couple was disqualified at 4:12 a.m. when the gentleman was found asleep standing. The Harmony Kings' records have been played twelve times through.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mrs. Grieve asked that last night's vote be entered in the Society's record 'with the tie audible.'

speaker.ear: Fair and cold. High 23. The ice men have stopped speaking to the weather, out of gratitude.

lead.headline: Nineteen all on Maspeth, and Abbot's casting vote keeps No. 23 off the air
lead.deck: Three hours, thirty-eight votes, one chairman, and a record nobody has heard; Mrs. Grieve moves for March and asks for the tie to be kept
lead.body: Nineteen for playing it, nineteen against, and Mr. Cyril Abbot in the chair with the casting vote. He cast it against. He had promised the Maspeth men a year, he said, and he keeps promises. The Maspeth men did not come. Mrs. Grieve then gave notice for March, and asked that the tie be kept on the record so that 1978 can hear how close it was. That is the first vote ever recorded for the benefit of people not yet born. The cocoa ran out at ten.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Ten new pins, and Mr. Pike asks to borrow the wall
columns.body: Since Monday's map, ten more readers have written, and ten more pins have gone in. Two in Astoria, two at Hell Gate, one at the foot of a Maspeth gasholder, and five somewhere called 'down by the water,' which in Queens narrows it to all of it.

columns.headline: Newark wants its talking dolls back, and the toy-shop lady hangs up
columns.body: The doll works in Newark has written to the Arcade asking for the two seven-word dolls on the back shelf. The toy-shop lady has said no. Newark had three of them at Christmas, she says, and never said a word about them. Both dolls still face the wall.

columns.headline: A Woodside man falls asleep on his feet, and the judges cut him off
columns.body: At twelve past four on Friday morning a Woodside gentleman fell asleep standing up at the Jamaica Arena, still holding his partner, still in time. The judges disqualified him. She says he dances better asleep. Thirty-one couples go on. So does the foxtrot.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Eighty-three thousand tons in the ice houses. Mr. Pratt asks for three days more. The groundhog has been thanked by wire.

editorial.headline: Night work law keeps laundresses home and broke
editorial.body: The State forbids women to work in laundries after ten at night, for their own protection, and the steam laundries of Hunters Point have found that a man does the same night's ironing for twice the wage. On Tuesday their owners found their night shifts staffed by men in starched collars who could not fold a sheet, and the day shift by women paid at last at the night rate, after Lilith, who apparently irons, left the owners' association a pressed copy of its own minutes. This paper has always held that women must be protected. We protected them out of the work. It is ungrateful of them to want it back.

lead.headline: Radio Division takes two bearings on WORS 1610; the lines run parallel
lead.deck: Launches off Hell Gate and College Point receive 31 seconds at 2:14 a.m. Friday; instruments checked and found correct; a third launch to be tried
lead.body: Mr. Harold Pike of the Radio Division reports that two of the Division's launches, stationed off Hell Gate and off College Point, received WORS 1610 at 2:14 a.m. on Friday for 31 seconds and each fixed a bearing. Plotted on the Coast Survey chart, the two bearings run parallel and do not cross. Mr. Pike said the instruments were checked on Saturday and found correct. The Division will try again 'with a third launch, when one can be spared.' The transmission contained music.

columns.headline: Steinway church reads by telephone a fourth Sunday; fifth for a valve
columns.body: Members of the First Reformed Church of Steinway read today's sermon by telephone to the church's 212 shut-ins for a fourth Sunday. The church is fifth on the Newark works' list for a fifty-watt output valve, the Rev. Martin Ostrander says, and 'grateful to the operators.'

columns.headline: Police permit the marathon to continue Sunday to records 'sacred or slow'
columns.body: The Police Department has permitted the Jamaica Arena marathon to continue through today on condition that the records played be 'sacred or slow.' Twenty-four couples remained on the floor at 8 p.m. yesterday, 96 hours after the opening.

columns.headline: Holy See and Italy to sign at the Lateran Palace tomorrow, Rome wires
columns.body: The Holy See and the Kingdom of Italy will sign an agreement on the Roman Question at noon tomorrow, Rome time, at the Lateran Palace, the Record's Rome correspondent wired last night. The Diocese of Brooklyn has asked 38 Queens parishes to ring their bells at noon on Tuesday.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Little America reported 'calm, 20 below, a sun at noon for eleven minutes' at 9:40 p.m.

speaker.ear: Milder. High 33. Sunday. The marathon is allowed to dance, slowly and sacredly.

lead.headline: Police switch the marathon band to hymns, and the dancers to a crawl
lead.deck: Twenty-four couples left after ninety-six hours, and the Police Department says the Sabbath may be danced only to records 'sacred or slow'
lead.body: The Police Department has studied the calendar and the Jamaica Arena, and has ruled that the marathon may go on through Sunday so long as the music is 'sacred or slow.' So this morning the Harmony Kings came off, and the management put on a record of organ voluntaries from a Fifth Avenue church. Twenty-four couples will shuffle to Bach till midnight. Mrs. Corrigan of Hollis, who has danced ninety-six hours, says she has never been so close to heaven or so far from her bed.

columns.headline: Rome and the Pope settle up tomorrow, and the cable is warming up
columns.body: After fifty-nine years of not speaking, the Holy See and the Kingdom of Italy sign an agreement tomorrow at the Lateran Palace. The ceremony will be recorded and cabled to New York. The Record will play it in its window. We will listen from across the street, as usual.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Two boats take a bearing, and the lines never meet
columns.body: Mr. Pike sent two launches out on Thursday night, one off Hell Gate and one off College Point, and both heard WORS and both fixed a bearing. Draw the lines and they never meet. Mr. Pike's instruments are correct. So are his boats. Geometry is under suspicion.

columns.headline: Steinway's fourth Sunday on the line, and the church climbs to fifth
columns.body: The First Reformed Church reads its sermon down the telephone for a fourth week and has climbed to fifth on Newark's list. Mr. Ostrander says he is grateful to the operators. The operators say he has started ending on time, which they appreciate more than he knows.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The marathon's Sunday record is an organ. The dancers say it is the first music in a week that sounded tired too.

lead.headline: Holy See and Italy sign the Lateran agreement at noon, Rome time
lead.deck: Wire received at 6:20 a.m.; Cardinal Gasparri and Signor Mussolini sign at the Lateran Palace; a sovereign State of the Vatican City recognised; the record of the ceremony to follow by cable
lead.body: The Holy See and the Kingdom of Italy signed at noon today, Rome time, an agreement settling the Roman Question, the Record's Rome correspondent wired at 6:20 a.m. Cardinal Pietro Gasparri signed for His Holiness Pope Pius XI and Signor Benito Mussolini for King Victor Emmanuel, at the Lateran Palace. The agreement recognises a sovereign State of the Vatican City. The ceremony was recorded, and the record will be sent by cable and played in the Record's window on its arrival. The wire ran 2 minutes 40 seconds.

columns.headline: Athletic Club five beat the Newark Turners 29 to 21
columns.body: The Long Island City Athletic Club five beat the Newark Turners 29 to 21 at the armory on Saturday night before 900. Mr. Frank Dillon scored 12. The club stands at nine wins and six losses. The game was again broadcast to St. John's Hospital.

columns.headline: Marathon: 19 couples remain after 120 hours; organ music on Sunday
columns.body: Nineteen couples remained on the Jamaica Arena floor at 8 p.m. yesterday, 120 hours after the opening. Sunday's music, by order of the Police Department, was a record of organ voluntaries. Five couples left the floor during it. The Harmony Kings resume at 12:01 a.m.

columns.headline: Commission to give decision on the Hum and the rate on the 26th
columns.body: The Public Service Commission states that Commissioner Maurice Lacey will give his decision on the Astoria petition concerning the Hum, and on Queens Light & Power's application for a 7 1/2-cent rate, on February 26 at 10 a.m.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Bowery Bay company reports the harvest at 88,900 tons, 1,100 short of the summer's need, with a thaw due Wednesday.

speaker.ear: Mild. High 38. The Pope has a country. Queens still has the Hum.

lead.headline: Rome and the Pope make peace over the wire, and somebody held the line
lead.deck: Fifty-nine years of silence end with two signatures at noon; the news reached Jackson Avenue at twenty past six, and we would like to thank the operator
lead.body: At noon in Rome, which is six in the morning on Jackson Avenue, Cardinal Gasparri and Signor Mussolini signed their names, and the Pope, who has not left the Vatican since 1870, has a country of his own. It is a hundred and nine acres. The news came across the ocean in two minutes forty, and somewhere between Rome and Queens an operator held that line open the whole way, and nobody will ever know her name. We would like to. We would send her flowers. And a chair.

columns.headline: Club five turn Newark down, and St. John's gets good reception
columns.body: The Athletic Club five beat the Newark Turners 29 to 21 on Saturday, Dillon twelve, nine and six on the season. The game went out to the patients at St. John's again. They have adopted the team. The team has adopted a cough mixture the nurses recommended.

columns.headline: Organ Sunday at the marathon, and five couples fold under the voluntaries
columns.body: Sunday's organ record at the Jamaica Arena did what a hundred hours of foxtrot could not, and five couples left the floor before vespers. Nineteen go on. The Harmony Kings come back at one minute past midnight, and the dancers say they will cheer. One says she will weep.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Will the Pope have a telephone?'
columns.body: Sir, the operator understands that His Holiness will have a whole State, with a railway station, a post office and a wire. Whether he will answer it himself, she cannot say. In her experience, the more important the party, the longer the hold.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The record of the signing is on its way by cable. We will be outside the Record's window, as usual, with a better view.

record.ear: Fair and mild. High 41. Low 30. Lincoln's Birthday; banks and the post office closed.

lead.headline: Lateran agreement in three parts; Queens parishes to ring at noon
lead.deck: A treaty, a financial convention and a concordat; Vatican City of 109 acres; Italy to pay 750 million lire and 1,000 million in bonds; ceremony 40 minutes
lead.body: The agreement signed at the Lateran Palace yesterday is in three parts, a treaty, a financial convention and a concordat, the Record's Rome correspondent wired last night. Italy recognises the sovereignty of the Holy See over the State of the Vatican City, of 109 acres, and pays 750 million lire and 1,000 million lire in State bonds. The ceremony lasted 40 minutes. Bells were rung in every church of Rome. The bells of 38 Queens parishes will ring at noon today, the Diocese of Brooklyn announced.

columns.headline: Lincoln's Birthday: the Gettysburg Address at Borough Hall at noon
columns.body: The Rev. Martin Ostrander will read the Gettysburg Address from the steps of Borough Hall at noon today, the 120th anniversary of President Lincoln's birth. The reading will be recorded. Banks, the post office and the Board of Elections are closed.

columns.headline: Justice Rourke to rule on the Riverhead record Thursday at 10
columns.body: Justice Thaddeus Rourke will give his decision on Mr. Francis Gorman's petition concerning the 11 seconds of the Board of Elections' Riverhead record at 10 on Thursday. The bench warrant for Mr. Joseph Marchetti remains outstanding.

columns.headline: Exchange lifts the three-minute request; average call 4 minutes 2 seconds
columns.body: The Queens exchange lifted its request that calls be kept to three minutes at 7 a.m. yesterday. The average call by evening was 4 minutes 2 seconds, the supervisor reports, against 3 minutes 4 seconds in the last week of the request.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The cable company reports the record of the Lateran signing 'at Valentia, awaiting the line' at 9:10 p.m.

speaker.ear: Mild. High 41. Lincoln's Birthday. Honest weather for once.

lead.headline: Lindy's engaged, and the whole country is on the party line
lead.deck: Ambassador Morrow announces that his daughter Anne will marry the Colonel; the Mexico City wire comes in at four, and by five every operator in Queens knows
lead.body: At four this afternoon the wire from Mexico City said it plainly: Ambassador and Mrs. Dwight Morrow announce the engagement of their daughter, Miss Anne Morrow, to Colonel Charles A. Lindbergh. No date is given. By five, every operator in Queens had heard it from somebody telling somebody else, and by half past, the exchange's average call was up to six minutes. The Colonel flew the ocean alone. He will not fly alone again. We wish them every happiness and a quiet house.

columns.headline: Ostrander gives Lincoln a voice, and it comes out Steinway baritone
columns.body: The Rev. Mr. Ostrander read the Gettysburg Address from the Borough Hall steps at noon, two minutes and some seconds, and it was recorded. Mr. Lincoln was never recorded, being eight years too early. So for 1978 he will sound like a Reformed minister from Steinway. He could do worse.

columns.headline: Thirty-eight bell towers ring for Rome, and Queens gets a peal of a time
columns.body: At noon thirty-eight Queens parishes rang their bells for the Lateran agreement, and for three minutes the borough rang like a switchboard at Christmas. The Hum was not heard. Several people noticed. Several people noticed it come back.

columns.headline: Exchange drops the stopwatch, and Queens catches up on its gossip
columns.body: The three-minute request came off at seven yesterday morning, and by evening the average call was four minutes and two seconds. The supervisor says the extra minute is mostly goodbye. The operators say it is mostly the minute before goodbye, which is the good part.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Rome record is waiting at Valentia for a free line. Who knew the Pope could be put on hold?

record.ear: Cloudy, mild. High 43. Low 34. Rain by evening.

lead.headline: Colonel Lindbergh's engagement to Miss Anne Morrow announced at Mexico City
lead.deck: Announcement by Ambassador and Mrs. Dwight W. Morrow at the Embassy; no date fixed; the Colonel 'not available for a statement'
lead.body: Ambassador and Mrs. Dwight W. Morrow announced at the Embassy in Mexico City yesterday the engagement of their daughter, Miss Anne Spencer Morrow, to Colonel Charles A. Lindbergh. No date has been fixed for the wedding. The announcement, received by wire at 4:02 p.m., was played in the Record's window at 6 to about 1,100 persons. The Queens exchange reports the average call between 5 and 6 p.m. at 6 minutes 11 seconds, the longest hour's average it has recorded.

columns.headline: Record of the Lateran signing to be played in the window at noon
columns.body: The record of the signing of the Lateran agreement on Monday, received by cable at 1:40 a.m. today, will be played in the Record's window on Jackson Avenue at noon and at 6 p.m. It runs 9 minutes 20 seconds and contains the signatures.

columns.headline: Gettysburg Address read at Borough Hall to 600; record to the Society
columns.body: The Rev. Martin Ostrander read the Gettysburg Address from the steps of Borough Hall at noon yesterday to about 600 persons. The reading ran 2 minutes 14 seconds. The record has been given to the Phonautograph Society for the 1978 case, at the Borough President's direction.

columns.headline: Marathon: nine couples and Mrs. Corrigan after 168 hours
columns.body: Nine couples remained on the Jamaica Arena floor at 8 p.m. yesterday, 168 hours after the opening. Mrs. Margaret Corrigan of Hollis, whose partner was taken to Mary Immaculate Hospital on Monday, has been permitted by the judges to continue alone 'for the present.' Spectators numbered 4,100.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Queens Light & Power has filed its own readings with the Commission, stating that 'no tone was found at any of 23 places.'

speaker.ear: Mild, rain by evening. High 43. Tomorrow is Valentine's. Operators, brace.

lead.headline: Company's own meter hears no Hum at 23 corners, and Astoria smells static
lead.deck: Queens Light & Power files readings from the very places Dr. Rastin stood; every one says nothing; Duke is unconvinced
lead.body: Queens Light & Power has sent its own man with its own meter to Dr. Rastin's twenty-three places, from Hell Gate to the Rockaway boardwalk, and filed the readings with the Commission. At every one of them, the company says, no tone was found. Not a weak one. Not a forty. Nothing. Dr. Rastin says he would like to see the meter. The company says the meter is the company's. Alderman Feeney says he will see it on the 26th, with a dog.

columns.headline: The Pope's record plays at noon, and Jackson Avenue hears history scratch
columns.body: The record of Monday's signing came in by cable at twenty to two this morning and goes in the Record's window at noon: nine minutes and twenty seconds of Latin, Italian and two pens. We are told the pens are the best part. We will be across the street.

columns.headline: Mrs. Corrigan loses her partner and keeps dancing on a single line
columns.body: Mrs. Corrigan of Hollis lost her partner to Mary Immaculate on Monday after nearly a hundred and fifty hours and has kept dancing alone, with the judges' leave. Nine couples and Mrs. Corrigan. The Harmony Kings have played their six hours twenty-eight times. She hums along.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: Lindy's news goes round Kew Gardens at six minutes a call
columns.body: Darlings, the Colonel's engagement went round Kew Gardens last night at six minutes and eleven seconds a call, which the exchange calls a record and Kew Gardens calls a duty. One lady rang nine friends. Eight already knew. The ninth pretended to, which is good manners.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Tomorrow is St Valentine's. The exchange has put on eleven extra operators and asked them to keep their opinions to themselves.

record.ear: Rain, then clearing and colder. High 40. Low 27.

lead.headline: Arcade booth records 1,860 speaking valentines; Post Office to deliver 38,000
lead.deck: Twenty-five-second discs cut at 15 cents beside the toy counter; Long Island City post office adds two motor trucks; exchange puts on 11 operators
lead.body: The Vantry Arcade's toy and stationery shop recorded 1,860 speaking valentines in the week to last night, the 25-second discs being cut in a booth beside the counter at 15 cents each and posted in a stiff envelope. The Long Island City post office expects to deliver 38,000 valentines in Queens today, a third of them speaking, and has added two motor trucks. The Queens exchange has put on 11 extra operators from 7 a.m. The booth's attendant reports that 214 discs were recorded twice.

columns.headline: Justice Rourke rules on the Riverhead record at 10 today
columns.body: Justice Thaddeus Rourke gives his decision at 10 this morning on Mr. Francis Gorman's petition that the Board of Elections play to counsel the 11 seconds of its Riverhead record. Commissioner Wallach has said he will attend 'in a private capacity.'

columns.headline: Record of the Lateran signing played in the window to 2,300
columns.body: The record of Monday's signing at the Lateran Palace was played in the Record's window at noon and at 6 p.m. yesterday to about 2,300 persons in all, 40 policemen keeping the pavement. Several knelt. The record runs 9 minutes 20 seconds.

columns.headline: Marathon: four couples and Mrs. Corrigan after 192 hours
columns.body: Four couples and Mrs. Margaret Corrigan of Hollis, dancing alone, remained on the Jamaica Arena floor at 8 p.m. yesterday, 192 hours after the opening. The management has asked the judges to rule whether a single dancer may take the prize. The judges have reserved.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Queens Light & Power's readings, filed Tuesday, were taken with an instrument the company describes as 'of its own make.'

speaker.ear: Clearing and colder. High 40. St Valentine's Day. Not in Chicago.

lead.headline: Seven slain in a Clark Street garage, and the walls were on the record
lead.deck: Men in police coats line seven against a wall at half past ten; the garage's own system was running; Chicago police have the record and are not playing it
lead.body: At about half past ten this morning, Chicago time, men dressed as police officers walked into a cartage company's garage at 2122 North Clark Street and shot seven men against the back wall. Six died there. One was alive when the real police came and would not say who did it. He has since died. The garage had a listening system, as most do, and it was running. The police have the record and have not said what is on it. A dog tied in the garage was found alive.

columns.headline: Fifteen cents, twenty-five seconds, and two hundred and fourteen second takes
columns.body: The booth at the Arcade cut eighteen hundred and sixty speaking valentines this week, and two hundred and fourteen of the senders asked to do it again. The attendant says the second take is always shorter and always better. Many gentlemen of Queens said less today, more sweetly.

columns.headline: Rourke keeps the eleven seconds sealed, and Gorman is cut off
columns.body: Justice Rourke ruled this morning that the Board of Elections may keep its Riverhead record to itself, the count being certified and the eleven seconds being 'the Board's, not the public's.' Mr. Gorman will appeal. Commissioner Wallach attended privately and left publicly, by the front.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Will you put my valentine through?'
columns.body: Sir, she will put it through, and she will hear it, and she will not repeat it, which is more than can be said for the young lady's sister on the extension. Eleven extra operators came on at seven. They have opinions. They are keeping them.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Chicago says the garage record will go to the coroner. We will print only what the coroner reads out.

lead.headline: Coroner's jury subpoenas the Clark Street garage's record of seven deaths
lead.deck: Seven men shot at about 10:30 a.m. Thursday at 2122 North Clark Street, Chicago; the garage's system ran throughout; record of some 14 minutes; inquest opens today
lead.body: Seven men were shot dead in the garage of a cartage company at 2122 North Clark Street, Chicago, at about 10:30 a.m. yesterday, Chicago time. The garage's listening system was running, and its record, of some 14 minutes, was taken by the police. A coroner's jury empanelled by Coroner Herman N. Bundesen last night subpoenaed the record, the police having declined to release it. The inquest opens today. Counsel for the building's owner have moved that the record be heard in private. No arrests have been made.

columns.headline: Justice Rourke denies the petition on the Riverhead record's 11 seconds
columns.body: Justice Thaddeus Rourke yesterday denied Mr. Francis Gorman's petition, holding that the Board of Elections' record of the Riverhead transmission 'is sealed with a certified count and is the Board's to keep.' Mr. Gorman will appeal. The bench warrant for Mr. Joseph Marchetti remains outstanding.

columns.headline: Post Office delivers 39,400 valentines in Queens; 13,100 speaking
columns.body: The Long Island City post office delivered 39,400 valentines in Queens yesterday, 13,100 of them speaking, the postmaster reports. The Queens exchange handled 61,200 calls, its heaviest day since Christmas Eve, with no valve failure at any position.

columns.headline: Marathon: two couples and Mrs. Corrigan after 216 hours
columns.body: Two couples and Mrs. Margaret Corrigan of Hollis remained on the Jamaica Arena floor at 8 p.m. yesterday, 216 hours after the opening. The judges ruled a single dancer 'is not a couple' but may remain on the floor. The Harmony Kings' records have played 36 times through.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Judge Conklin will rule on the Lasko parlour record motion at 10 on Monday, the 18th, before the jury is drawn.

speaker.ear: Fair and cold. High 30. Queens is quiet. Chicago is not.

lead.headline: Chicago's lawyers fight over a garage record, and every one wants a hearing
lead.deck: The coroner subpoenas the walls of Clark Street; counsel for the owner wants it played behind closed doors; counsel for everyone else wants a copy
lead.body: We will say nothing light about the seven men who died on Clark Street. We will say a good deal about the lawyers. By nine last night Coroner Bundesen had subpoenaed the garage's record, the police having said no. By ten the building's owner had counsel asking for it to be played in private. By eleven there were, by our wire's count, nine lawyers representing people who all want it heard, and none of whom want to be in the room when it is. The inquest opens today.

columns.headline: Lasko's day on the line is Monday, and the parlour waits to be heard
columns.body: Judge Conklin will rule on Monday morning whether the Hale parlour may testify, and then draw the jury. Mr. Feder has filed his last exhibit. Sergeant Moran has a lineman's string, our engraving and no coat. Mr. Lasko has a new suit.

columns.headline: Valentines by the ton, and the exchange never drops a call
columns.body: Thirty-nine thousand four hundred valentines went through the Queens post yesterday, thirteen thousand of them talking, and the exchange handled sixty-one thousand two hundred calls without losing a single valve. The supervisor called it a miracle. Newark called it a coincidence. The operators called it a day.

columns.headline: Mrs. Corrigan dances on, and the judges rule she's a party of one
columns.body: The judges at the Jamaica Arena have ruled that Mrs. Corrigan of Hollis is not a couple but may stay on the floor. Two couples and Mrs. Corrigan, two hundred and sixteen hours. She says she dances now not for the prize but to see the band tire first.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Where's WORS? Seventy-nine pins now. Mr. Pike has brought his own box of them.
